meta.description: Credited to Pelé — he even tweeted it in 2014 — but no book, speech, or interview documents the exact wording. Honest attribution, no pinned source.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1940–2022 · Brazilian footballer · three-time World Cup winner
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Pelé, and he endorsed it himself — his verified account posted the opening line in July 2014. But no book, speech, or interview documents the exact wording, and the popular claim that it comes from his 1977 autobiography is unverified.

source.excerpt: Success is no accident. It is hard work, perseverance, learning, studying, sacrifice and most of all, love of what you are doing or learning to do.
trail: The full line — “…and most of all, love of what you are doing or learning to do” — is carried on Goodreads ↗ with no book or source, under a notice that quotes there are community-added and “not verified.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its general quotes section with no citation — it is not placed in a sourced section, and not flagged as misattributed either.
PassItOn ↗ and other inspiration sites reproduce it attributed to Pelé but cite no book, speech, or interview.

Pelé’s own verified X account posted the opening wording on 22 July 2014 (status 491679674742104065, whose timestamp decodes to that date) — strong evidence he embraced the line, though it does not establish where or when he first said it.
source.excerptNote: The circulated line is longer than the popular truncation; the version ending at “sacrifice” is a shortened form. No source page or edition is ever cited for either.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento)
source.rightsNote: This is a modern statement — its earliest documented appearances are c. 2013–2014, including Pelé’s own 2014 X post — so it is well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff and rests with Pelé’s estate. Because no specific published work is confirmed, treat the copyright as attaching to Pelé’s modern authorship rather than to any one edition; there is no basis to call it public-domain.

author.name: Pelé
author.heading: About Pelé
author.metaLine: 1940–2022 · Brazilian footballer · three-time World Cup winner
author.bio: Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento, 1940–2022) is regarded as one of the greatest footballers in history, winning the World Cup with Brazil in 1958, 1962, and 1970. After his playing career he became a global ambassador for the sport and a fixture of motivational culture — which is part of why aspirational one-liners gravitate to his name. He was active on social media in his later years and did publicly share this very line.

misattribution.heading: The sourcing problem
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Pelé is credible — he himself posted the line — but the “source” you will see attached to it is not.

items.who: “Pelé: My Life and the Beautiful Game” (1977)
items.why: Many reposts assert the line comes from Pelé’s 1977 autobiography, but no page or edition is ever cited, and the wording does not surface in the record until quote aggregators picked it up around 2013–2014. Treat the book citation as unconfirmed rather than established.
The line is reproduced on Goodreads ↗ and similar aggregators with the author name but no book, date, or context — Goodreads even warns its quotes are community-added and “not verified.”

misattribution.truthLine: What is solid: the line is genuinely a Pelé line — his Wikiquote ↗ page carries it and his verified account posted it in 2014. What is not solid is any claim about which book, speech, or year it ‘originally’ came from.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Pelé
lead: Pelé is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: a globally beloved figure whose name lends instant authority to any tidy sentence about effort and success. Unlike most magnet attributions, though, this line has a real anchor — Pelé publicly shared it himself — which is why it lands as “attributed” rather than “fabricated.”

The catch is that a genuine attribution and a documented source are two different things. Here the first is present and the second is missing: no page of a book, no dated interview, no speech. The honest answer is that Pelé embraced the line, but where and when he first said it remains undocumented.
context.pull: Genuinely his to say — but nobody can tell you which page it came from.
